title: The water snake
hookLine: grasping the teaching wrongly is like grabbing a snake by the tail (MN 22)

cards: Grab a snake by the tail, and it whips around and bites the hand that's holding it. Pin it first with a forked stick, a branch with a V at one end, then take it behind the head, and it can't.
In MN 22 that simple tool is the difference between being bitten and walking away safe. And the Buddha used the picture for something unexpected: how people hold on to his own teaching.

teach.b: MN 22, the Alagaddupama, the simile of the water snake, begins with a monk named Arittha. He had come to a wrong view: that the things the Buddha called obstacles weren't really obstacles to someone who indulged in them.
The other monks tried to talk him out of it. He held on. So the Buddha called him in, and was blunt: misguided man, when have you ever heard me teach it that way?
Then he turned to everyone. Some people, he said, learn the teaching, the discourses, the verses, the stories, but don't examine its meaning with wisdom.
They learn it to criticize others and win arguments, and so it harms them, like a man looking for a water snake who finds a big one and grabs it by the coils or by the tail.

teach.h: GRABBED BY THE TAIL, IT BITES.
teach.b: It turns and bites his hand or his arm, and he suffers, even to death, because he grasped it wrongly.
Others learn the teaching, examine its meaning, and don't use it to win arguments, and it leads to their welfare for a long time.

teach.h: PINNED, THEN HELD BY THE NECK.
teach.b: Like a man who pins the snake down with a forked stick, then takes it firmly by the neck. It can coil all over his arm, and it won't bite.

So the danger isn't in the teaching. It's in the grip. The Dhammapada has a line for someone who knows the words without living them, in Max Müller's translation: “like a cowherd counting the cows of others.”

how: Teachers cite the water snake simile as a warning against studying the teaching for debate or status, and encourage students to apply what they learn to themselves first.

o: a cobra charmed by a snake handler's pipe
a water snake: it bites when held wrongly
a dragon guarding treasure under a lake

p: held on to a wrong view

s: the simile says the teaching itself is dangerous
the danger is in the grip: learning it to criticize and win arguments.
MN 22 warns against learning the teaching to win arguments
that's the wrong grip that gets you bitten.
the Buddha gently agreed with Arittha
he called him a misguided man and corrected the view.

games.q: you've found a big water snake and you need to catch it. what does the wise man in MN 22 do?
o: grab it by the tail, fast
pin it with a forked stick, then hold it by the neck
games.why: pin first, then hold behind the head. it can coil all over his arm and it won't bite. that's the right grip on a teaching.

practice: Hold in mind one teaching that matters to you, from this path or anywhere in your life, and check your grip: do you use it mostly to look at yourself, or to measure other people?
No verdict needed; just notice where your hand is, on the tail or behind the head, then let it rest, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: alagadda. A teaching grasped wrongly bites; held rightly, for understanding and not for winning, it helps.

orig.note: Pali alagadda: a water snake, the snake of MN 22's simile.

carryVoice: Your line: hold it rightly. The same words can heal or bite, depending on the hand. See you tomorrow.
